opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. When I look back, my path into AI wasn't one big decision. It was a series of small curiosities that kept pulling me in the same direction.

I grew up in Taiwan and studied electrical engineering. Back then, AI wasn't the hot topic it is today. What fascinated me was signals and images: how a machine could take in raw pixels and somehow make sense of them. That question, how you get from numbers to meaning, is really what got me started.

Then I went to the University of Maryland for my PhD and worked on computer vision. That was before deep learning took over, so we were doing a lot of hand-designed features, graphical models, optimization. In hindsight that was valuable training. It taught me to think carefully about the structure of a problem instead of just throwing data at it.

After graduating I joined an industrial research lab, Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs, and worked on more applied vision problems: robotics, detection, things that had to actually work. Around that time deep learning really exploded. I remember feeling both excited and a bit anxious, because the field was changing under our feet. I had to decide whether to keep doing what I knew or jump into the new paradigm. I jumped.

Then I joined NVIDIA, and the focus shifted from understanding images to generating them. That was a big change in mindset for me. With recognition, you ask the machine to describe the world. With generation, you ask it to imagine the world. Work on GANs, image-to-image translation, and later GauGAN came from that. To generate something realistic, the model has to capture the structure of the world in a deeper way.

So if I summarize my path, it's a journey from perception to imagination, and now toward simulation: building models that understand how the physical world works, so that robots and other physical AI systems can learn from them. Looking back, I think the common thread is that I've always been interested in one question. Can a machine build an internal model of the world? Every stage of my career has been a different angle on that question.

r001.rationale: He describes his path into AI as a series of small curiosities and traces how successive experiences in vision, applied research, deep learning, and generative models drew him further into the field.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I don't think my path was planned so much as it unfolded one curiosity at a time.

I grew up in Taiwan, and as a student I was drawn to signal processing and computer vision long before anyone called it "AI." At National Taiwan University I was fascinated by the idea that you could take an image, which is just a grid of numbers, and have a machine understand something about the world from it. That felt almost magical to me, and the magic never wore off.

I went to the University of Maryland for my PhD, and that was the period when the field was still mostly hand-designed features and probabilistic models. Deep learning hadn't taken over yet. Honestly, that turned out to be a gift, because I learned to think about the structure of problems rather than just throwing data at them. When the deep learning wave came, I had a foundation to make sense of why it worked.

After my PhD I joined Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs, and later NVIDIA, where I've been for about a decade now. At NVIDIA I found what I'd call my real subject: generative models. Work like UNIT, pix2pixHD, GauGAN, and later the whole line toward world models and simulation. What ties all of it together is a single question that has stayed with me since graduate school. Can a machine not just recognize the world, but imagine it? Can it synthesize what it hasn't seen, in a way that is consistent with physics and with how things actually look?

So if I had to describe my path, I'd say it moved from understanding images, to generating images, to generating worlds. Each step felt like the natural next question rather than a career decision. And I think that's the honest answer: I followed the problems that wouldn't leave me alone, and the field happened to grow up around them.

r001.rationale: He describes his path as unfolding “one curiosity at a time,” moving from early interest in signal processing and computer vision through graduate study and later generative-model work, with each step leading to the next.

astra-6.text:
I think of my path into artificial intelligence as a gradual process of following my curiosity. What interests me is how we can turn something that feels intuitive to people—recognizing a scene, understanding an image, imagining something new—into a problem a machine can learn to solve.

That also shapes how I think about research. You start with a question, try an idea, and learn from the gap between what you expected and what actually happened. Over time, those questions give you a direction. So I see my path less as a fixed plan and more as a series of questions that keep opening up new possibilities.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gradual, curiosity-driven path and evolving research questions, but does not say that his interest developed through successive encounters with the field.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a path shaped by curiosity. What drew me toward artificial intelligence was the question of how a machine could learn from examples and use that experience to handle something new. Vision makes that question especially tangible: we understand so much simply by looking, yet explaining how we do it is remarkably difficult.

For me, the appeal is moving between that fundamental question and the practical work of building something. You have an idea about learning, you test it, and the results expose what you still don’t understand. That cycle of curiosity, experimentation, and revision is how I would describe my path into AI.

r001.rationale: The response describes curiosity about machine learning and an experimentation cycle, but does not say Liu’s interest developed through successive encounters with the field.
